The hull is chosen, not designed. Its beam is the trunk's beam and cannot exceed it, which fixes what the boat can ever be before a tool touches it.

steamer: The keel goes down first: a line of heavy iron plates along the bottom on the centreline, with the stem and sternpost at its ends. Every frame is set out from it.

Rolled iron frames on a keel plate. Iron does not care about the length of a tree, which is the whole point: a wooden hull is limited to about 60 m by the timber available and by hogging, and iron simply is not.
Plates riveted to the frames, lapped and caulked. A riveted seam is watertight and, unlike a caulked one, does not need re-caulking every few years — which is a large part of why iron won.
The deck is laid, and its beams tie the two sides together. Added at this stage: a rudder hung at the stern, a funnel, a superstructure, a bridge, anchors and boats.

Four masts are stepped. The forward three are each built in three pieces, lower mast, topmast and topgallant mast; the aftermost mast is built in two pieces, lower mast and topmast. Each piece above the lowest stands in the doubling at the head of the one below, held up by an iron fid through its heel, so it can be lowered to the deck. Also added: tops at the lower mastheads, crosstrees at the topmast heads, crosstrees at the lower masthead of the gaff mast, a bowsprit and cowl ventilators.

Shrouds run from each masthead down to the hull and hold each mast against the sideways pull of the sail. Stays hold them fore and aft. Ratlines across the shrouds make a ladder for the crew to climb aloft. Also added: channels outside the hull and deadeyes with their lanyards.

The square-rigged masts cross 12 yards; the square sails hang from them. Braces at the yardarms swing the yards round to trim the sails to the wind. One gaff and one boom go up: a gaff holds the head of a fore-and-aft sail and a boom its foot. The running rigging is rove: halyards, sheets, tacks and four more kinds of line. Also added: trusses, parrels and blocks.
The sails are bent on: square sails on the forward three, a gaff sail on the aftermost mast and three headsails on the stays forward.
dreadnought: The keel goes down first: a line of heavy steel plates along the bottom on the centreline, with the stem and sternpost at its ends. Every frame is set out from it.

Mild-steel frames on a keel plate, erected one by one and faired by eye — the block-built hull is a post-war invention. Steel displaced iron in the 1880s because it is stronger for the same weight, so the same ship needs fewer tons of hull.

Plates riveted to the frames, lapped at every land. Titanic carried three million rivets, driven by four-man gangs — hydraulic where the shell was fair enough, by hand round the bow and stern where the machine could not reach.
The weather deck closes the hull. Added at this stage: rudder, two funnels and superstructure.
